sermon:
## Before I Formed You
*Called by a knowing that came before you were ready*

**Text:** Jeremiah 1 · **Supporting:** Psalm 139:13-16 · Isaiah 49:1 · 1 Corinthians 1:27-29 · Galatians 1:15

Every call you have ever heard in church starts with you. Your gifts, your readiness, your willingness, your yes. So when God comes to a young man in a collapsing nation and tells him to speak, you expect the same opening, and you do not get it. You get something older than the man himself.

**The call rests on God's prior knowing**
The word does not begin with Jeremiah's qualifications. It begins behind him. "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations." (Jeremiah 1:5) Read it slowly. Three verbs, all of them God's, all of them finished before the boy drew breath, knew, consecrated, appointed. Jeremiah contributes nothing to the foundation of his own call. He is not chosen because he is ready. He is told he was set apart before he was anything at all. This is the same ground David stood on when he wrote, "you knitted me together in my mother's womb… your eyes saw my unformed substance." (Psalm 139:13-16) It is the ground Isaiah's servant stood on: "The LORD called me from the womb." (Isaiah 49:1) The call is not a reward for a finished man. It is a verdict spoken over an unfinished one.

And Jeremiah does what every honest person does when God names a calling bigger than the self. He objects. "Ah, Lord GOD. Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth." (Jeremiah 1:6) Notice he is not lying. He really cannot speak. He really is young. The objection is true. It simply is not the point. God does not argue with the facts of Jeremiah's weakness. He overrules their relevance. The same God who told Moses at the bush, "I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak," is the God who steps over Jeremiah's "I am only a youth" without conceding the premise. Weakness was never the disqualifier. It was the canvas.

And the year matters, because this is not a comfortable call. Jeremiah is sent in the thirteenth year of Josiah's reign, around 627 BC, into the last decades of a nation about to be swallowed by Babylon. Within forty years the temple will be ash. He is being commissioned to preach to a people who will not listen, in a kingdom that will not survive, and God tells him so up front: "they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail against you." (Jeremiah 1:19) Not they will repent. They will fight. The call comes with the cost printed on it.

**The fear is answered by presence, not removed by ease**
Watch what God does not say. He does not say, do not be afraid, this will be easy. He does not say, the people will listen, the kings will repent, your family will stand with you. None of that is coming, and God knows it. What he says instead is this: "Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you, declares the LORD." (Jeremiah 1:8) The fear is not treated as a problem to be solved by improving the circumstances. It is answered by a person who refuses to leave. Then God touches his mouth, "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth" (1:9), and the content of the commission lands with terrible weight: "to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant." (1:10) Four verbs of demolition before two of construction. This is not a man being sent to grow a movement. He is being sent to announce a collapse, and to wait, on the far side of it, for a planting he may never see.

Paul understood this floor under the call. God, he wrote, "chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise… so that no human being might boast in the presence of God." (1 Corinthians 1:27-29) And of his own commission: God "set me apart before I was born." (Galatians 1:15) The same word over Jeremiah is the word over Paul. The call never depended on the readiness of the called. And then God hands Jeremiah two visions to confirm it, an almond branch and a boiling pot, because the prophet who doubts his own adequacy needs to know whose word he carries. "I am watching over my word to perform it." (1:12) The pressure is not on Jeremiah to make the word come true. God watches over it himself. Jeremiah only has to say it.

**What this asks of us**
Here is where I have to stop describing Jeremiah and tell the truth about us. We have built a whole Christian culture on the opposite foundation. We wait to feel ready. We wait to feel qualified, equipped, healed enough, sure enough, and we call that waiting humility. It is not humility. It is a quieter form of the same self-trust, because it still makes the call depend on us. I have done this. I have hidden behind "I'm not ready" when the honest sentence was "I'm not willing to be hurt for this." Jeremiah's youth was real. So is your inadequacy. God is not impressed by it and he is not stopped by it, because he never asked you to be the foundation. He is.

And this is the line that runs straight to Christ. Before you were formed, you were known, and the knowing was not neutral. It cost. The One who knew you before the womb is the One who was "destined before the foundation of the world" to be the Lamb, who went under the plucking up and the breaking down himself so there could be a building and a planting on the other side. Jeremiah's commission was a shadow of it: demolition, then construction. Christ is the order completed. He was torn down so you could be planted. Your call does not rest on your strength. It rests on a knowing older than you and a death older than your sin.

You were known before you were ready.

## Two Evils, Broken Cisterns
*The double sin of leaving the spring to dig a hole*

**Text:** Jeremiah 2:1-13 · **Supporting:** John 4:13-14 · Psalm 36:9 · Isaiah 55:1-2 · John 7:37-38

Most of us think of sin as one thing, a wrong done, a line crossed. Jeremiah will not let us keep it that simple. He stands Israel in front of the charge and names not one evil but two, and the second is worse than the first.

**The first evil: leaving the fountain**
God opens not with anger but with memory. "I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed me in the wilderness." (Jeremiah 2:2) Before the indictment, the ache. This is a God recalling a marriage that has gone cold, asking the only honest question a betrayed love can ask: "What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me?" (2:5) What was lacking? What did I fail to be? The answer is nothing, and everyone in the room knows it. He brought them through the wilderness, into a plentiful land, and they ate its fruit, "but when you came in, you defiled my land." (2:7) So God names the first evil plainly: "they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters." (2:13) Fountain, a spring, water that moves, that comes up from a depth you did not dig and cannot exhaust. To forsake that is the first sin, and it is bad enough.

This is the very thing Jesus offered the woman at the well, the same image exactly: "everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life." (John 4:13-14) The psalmist had already named the source: "with you is the fountain of life." (Psalm 36:9) God is not one drink among many. He is the spring itself. Leaving the spring is evil number one.

And notice God does not begin the indictment with the sins themselves. He begins with the strangeness of it. "Has a nation changed its gods, even though they are no gods? But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit." (Jeremiah 2:11) Pagan nations stay loyal to gods that are not even real. Israel betrayed the God who actually delivered them. The prophet calls heaven itself to witness the absurdity: "Be appalled, O heavens, at this; be shocked, be utterly desolate." (2:12) The angels are summoned to stare at it, because nothing in creation should make this little sense, a people walking away from the only water there is.

**The second evil: digging the cistern**
But God does not stop at one. "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water." (Jeremiah 2:13) A cistern is not a spring. A cistern is a pit you carve out of rock to catch and store rainwater you do not control. It is labor, hewing stone is brutal work, and it is dependence on a far worse source. And these cisterns are cracked. They cannot even keep the little that is poured into them. So count the evils. First, they walked away from inexhaustible water that costs nothing. Second, they broke their backs digging a hole that leaks. They left the spring to manufacture the drought.

Hear what God is exposing. The tragedy is not only that we leave him. It is what we leave him for. Isaiah saw the same madness: "Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy?" (Isaiah 55:1-2) We do not trade up. We trade the river for a leaking bucket and then call it freedom. The career that was supposed to fill us. The relationship that was supposed to complete us. The achievement, the approval, the next thing, broken cisterns, all of them, dug at enormous cost, holding nothing.

And notice the word for themselves. They "hewed out cisterns for themselves." This is the whole anatomy of idolatry in one phrase. The cistern is self-made, self-controlled, self-maintained, water you do not have to depend on anyone else for, water you manage on your own terms. That is exactly its appeal and exactly its failure. The spring requires trust. The cistern requires only labor. And we will choose backbreaking self-sufficiency over restful dependence every single time, because dependence is the thing the human heart most despises. We would rather control a trickle than receive a flood.

**The truth we have to own**
And I have to be honest about how this works in me, because the second evil is the one I am proud of. The leaving, I can repent of leaving. But the cistern, the thing I built, the life I constructed to hold my own water, that I defend. I dug it. I am invested in it. The labor is the proof I am self-sufficient, and the leaking is precisely what I refuse to admit. We are most committed to the substitutes we worked hardest to make. That is why the spring is so hard to return to. Coming back means admitting the digging was wasted.

This is where Jesus stands in the temple and says the thing Jeremiah was waiting for someone to say. "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'" (John 7:37-38) Not a cistern you maintain. A river that flows out of you because the spring has moved in. The whole work of the cross is God refusing to let his bride die of thirst beside the holes she dug. He came to the well of our exhaustion, and he did not say, dig deeper. He said, come and drink. The water is free because it cost him everything.

We dig for what we already had.

## The Temple Will Not Save You
*When the sanctuary becomes a charm against the God who lives there*

**Text:** Jeremiah 7:1-15 · **Supporting:** 1 Samuel 4:3-11 · Micah 6:6-8 · Matthew 21:12-13 · Isaiah 1:11-17

Jeremiah is told to stand in the gate of the temple, the holiest spot in the nation, the place of guaranteed safety, and there, to people on their way in to worship, he is told to take that safety away.

**The deceptive words**
God gives him the exact sentence to confront. "Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.'" (Jeremiah 7:4) Said three times, the way people repeat a thing they are using as a charm. The logic was airtight to them. God's house is here. God will not let his own house fall. Therefore we are safe, whatever we do. The building had become a guarantee. And God answers the logic by attaching a condition to it they had quietly deleted: "if you truly amend your ways and your deeds, if you truly execute justice one with another, if you do not oppress the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow… then I will let you dwell in this place." (7:5-7) The presence was never unconditional. The charm was a lie.

Then comes the charge, and it is unbearable in its precision. "Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely… and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered', only to go on doing all these abominations?" (7:9-10) There is the whole machinery. Sin all week, appear at the house on the sabbath, claim deliverance, and go back to the sinning, using the worship as the very thing that licenses the wickedness. "Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?" (7:11)

**Shiloh's ruins**
The people thought the building made them untouchable. So God points them to a building that was not. "Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did to it because of the evil of my people Israel." (7:12) Shiloh, where the ark had rested, where the tabernacle stood for generations. The nation had once carried that ark into battle as a good-luck charm too, certain that God's box would save them, "that it may come among us and save us from the power of our enemies." (1 Samuel 4:3) The ark was captured. Israel was slaughtered. The holy object did not save the unholy people. And God says now: I did it to Shiloh, and I will do it to this place. "I will do to the house that is called by my name… as I did to Shiloh." (Jeremiah 7:14) Sacred space is not a shield. God will reduce his own sanctuary to rubble before he will be used as cover for injustice.

This is the oldest argument in the prophets. Micah had already cut to it: God does not want "thousands of rams, with ten thousands of rivers of oil", "he has told you, O man, what is good… to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God." (Micah 6:7-8) Isaiah heard God say of the festivals, "I cannot endure iniquity and solemn assembly… cease to do evil, learn to do good, seek justice." (Isaiah 1:13-17) The worship God hates most is the worship offered by hands that crush the widow on the way home.

And see exactly where God puts the test. Not in the volume of the sacrifices, not in the beauty of the liturgy, not in the orthodoxy of the prayers, in the treatment of three named people who can do nothing for you. "The sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow." (Jeremiah 7:6) The immigrant with no rights. The child with no father. The woman with no husband. God says the genuineness of your worship is measured at exactly the point where it can buy you nothing, how you treat the people who cannot repay you, cannot promote you, cannot even thank you in a way that counts. That is the gauge. Everything else can be faked. That cannot.

**The mirror turns**
Now I have to stop preaching at ancient Judah, because I know this den of robbers from the inside. I have stood in the holy place and used it to feel safe about a life that was not changing. I have preached sermons that were technically true while treating someone in my own congregation as a problem rather than a person, and then gone home certain I was a faithful man because the sermon was sound. That is the exact machinery of Jeremiah 7, the religious act used as cover for the unrepented life. We do it still. We are present, we are involved, we know the songs, we serve, and we treat the building and the busyness as proof we are fine, while the actual content of our days, how we treat the powerless, the sojourner, the people who can do nothing for us, goes untouched. We have made church attendance a cistern. We pour religion into it and call ourselves delivered. The temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD. God is not impressed by the volume of the chant.

And this is exactly the house Jesus walked into. He came to that same temple, overturned the tables, and quoted this very chapter back at it: "My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you make it a den of robbers." (Matthew 21:13) Then he said the thing that ends the whole system of sacred-space-as-charm: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up, speaking of his body. The building was never the safety. He is. He let himself be torn down, the true temple, so that no one would ever again have to hide behind walls. You cannot use Christ as a charm. He saves the people he actually changes.

Sacred walls cannot cover injustice.

## The Potter's House
*Sovereign hands, and the clay that answered no*

**Text:** Jeremiah 18:1-12 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 64:8 · Romans 9:20-21 · Jeremiah 18:12 · Ezekiel 18:30-32

God sends Jeremiah to a workshop to learn a doctrine with his eyes. Go down to the potter's house, and there I will let you hear my words. Not read them. Watch them.

**The freedom of the potter**
Jeremiah goes, and watches a vessel go wrong on the wheel. "The vessel he was making of clay was spoiled in the potter's hand, and he reworked it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to do." (Jeremiah 18:4) The clay resists, the shape collapses, and the potter does not throw it out, he presses it back into a lump and begins again. Then God gives the meaning: "O house of Israel, can I not do with you as this potter has done? Behold, like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel." (18:6) Here is sovereign freedom, stated as plainly as it is ever stated in Scripture. The clay does not instruct the potter. Isaiah confessed it: "we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand." (Isaiah 64:8) Paul drove it home against every complaint: "Who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, 'Why have you made me like this?'" (Romans 9:20-21) The hands are free. They will get what they intend.

**The freedom bound to response**
But Jeremiah is not preaching fatalism, and we have to be careful here, because the chapter does something most people miss. God binds his sovereign freedom to the people's response, not as a limit on his power, but as the shape his power takes. "If at any time I declare concerning a nation… that I will pluck up and break down and destroy it, and if that nation turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster." (18:7-8) And the reverse: "if it does evil… then I will relent of the good." (18:9-10) The Potter announces judgment precisely so that it can be averted. The threat is mercy in the form of a warning. This is the heart God revealed through Ezekiel: "I have no pleasure in the death of anyone… so turn, and live." (Ezekiel 18:32) The sovereignty is real. And it bends toward the turning.

So the whole chapter sets up a single moment, an offer. "Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way." (18:11) The wheel is still turning. The lump is still soft. Come back, and the marred vessel becomes something else in the same hands. This is what people miss when they fight the doctrine of the Potter, they hear tyranny, and the text is announcing mercy. A potter who simply wanted to destroy a spoiled vessel would say nothing. He would crush it and start over without warning. This Potter narrates his intentions out loud, in advance, precisely to give the clay a chance to soften. The announcement of judgment is itself the offer of escape from it.

**The clay that answered**
And then comes the most chilling verse in the passage, because the clay talks back. "But they say, 'That is in vain. We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart.'" (18:12) That is in vain. Hopeless. Don't bother. We will follow our own plans. The clay looks at the patient hands offering to remake it, and it says no. It chooses the marring. It would rather be its own ruined shape than the potter's new one. This is the verse that should stop us, because it is the most natural answer in the world.

I know it is, because it is mine. The doctrine of the Potter is the doctrine people fight hardest, and I understand the fight, it offends the part of us that wants to be self-made. But notice the offense is never in the verses where God offers to remake us. It is only ever in our refusal. "We will follow our own plans", that is not a theology of human dignity. It is the most stubborn enslavement there is, dressed as freedom. We call our resistance to God's reshaping "being true to ourselves," and what we are being true to is a vessel that is already spoiled on the wheel. The tragedy of Judah is not that the Potter was harsh. It is that the clay refused the hands that were trying to save it.

And I have to confess I have said it is in vain in my own words, more times than I want to count. Not out loud, not as a theology, but as a quiet operating assumption, that this particular fault in me is just who I am, that the marring is permanent, that God's hands have already moved on. That despair sounds like humility. It is not. It is the clay's stubbornness wearing the mask of low self-esteem. To say "I cannot be remade" is just another way of saying "I will follow my own plans," because both of them refuse the hands. The Potter never said the vessel was beyond reworking. We say it for him, and then call our resignation realism.

And this is where the gospel breaks the deadlock the clay cannot break. We are clay that says no, and God did not finally answer our no with destruction. He came down into the workshop. The Word became flesh, took on the clay himself, and on the cross the Potter let himself be marred for the vessels that defied him: "he was crushed for our iniquities." The only one who never resisted the Father's hands was broken in the place of all of us who did. That is how a stubborn lump gets remade, not by trying harder to be moldable, but by a new heart given, the heart of stone replaced with a heart of flesh. You cannot reshape yourself. You can only stop saying that it is in vain, and put yourself back in the hands.

The clay said no to the potter.

## The Fire and the Curse
*The honest agony of a man who could not stop and could not go on*

**Text:** Jeremiah 20:7-18 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 1:8 · Psalm 88:1-9 · 2 Corinthians 4:8-9 · Matthew 26:38-39

We have a category for the triumphant believer and a category for the fallen one. We do not have a good category for this: a faithful man, doing exactly what God called him to do, in such pain that he wishes he had never been born. Jeremiah 20 forces the category open.

**The word that burns**
The chapter opens with the cost. Jeremiah has been beaten and put in the stocks by a temple official for preaching what God gave him to preach. And out of that comes a confession so raw it barely sounds like Scripture. "O LORD, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed. I have become a laughingstock all the day; everyone mocks me." (Jeremiah 20:7) He accuses God of overpowering him into a vocation that has cost him everything. And then he tries the obvious solution, just stop. Stop preaching, stop saying the unwelcome word, and the mockery ends. He tries it. It does not work. "If I say, 'I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name,' there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot." (20:9) There is the first half of the truth. The word he hates to speak is a fire he cannot contain. Faithfulness here is not a feeling of victory. It is the inability to quit.

**The despair that curses the day**
And then, in the same breath, the same chapter, the prophet does something we are taught not to do in church. He does not edit his agony before God. The passage swings, for a moment he praises: "Sing to the LORD; praise the LORD. For he has delivered the life of the needy." (20:13) And then immediately, with no transition, no resolution, it crashes into the darkest words a believer can say. "Cursed be the day on which I was born. Let the day not be blessed on which my mother bore me." (20:14) "Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow, and spend my days in shame?" (20:18) Read those two halves together, praise, then the curse of his own birth, and refuse the urge to tidy it. Jeremiah holds them both. The fire and the curse. The call he cannot abandon and the despair so deep he wishes he had never lived to carry it.

This is not weak faith. This is faith honest enough to bring the whole self into the presence of God without cleaning it up first. The psalmist did it: "I am a man who has no strength… you have put me in the depths of the pit." (Psalm 88:4-6) That psalm ends in darkness, by the way, "darkness is my closest friend", and God put it in the songbook. He gave us words for the night and did not require us to skip to the morning.

And look closely at where Jeremiah aims the accusation. "O LORD, you have deceived me." He does not curse Babylon. He does not even mainly curse the men who beat him. He brings his complaint to God, against God, in the presence of God. That is the strange logic of biblical lament, it is the most God-soaked thing a sufferer can do, because the only person worth accusing is the one you still believe is sovereign over your pain. A man who had given up on God would not bother arguing with him. Jeremiah's complaint is itself a confession of faith. He is still talking to the one he holds responsible. The opposite of faith here is not the curse of the day of his birth. The opposite of faith is silence, walking away and never bringing the agony to God at all.

**The lie we tell about faithfulness**
Now the hard turn, and it is on us, the church. We have quietly taught people that this passage cannot happen. We have implied that if you are walking with God, you will not be in this kind of pain, and if you are in this kind of pain, something must be wrong with your faith. So the suffering believer gets handed the worst burden of all: the shame of suffering on top of the suffering. I have done it. I have rushed someone past their lament because their honesty made me uncomfortable, and I have called the rushing "encouragement." Jeremiah indicts that. The most faithful man in Judah was the one in the most pain, and the pain did not make him faithless. It made him faithful in the dark. We do not have permission to require people to skip this chapter.

And here is where the fire and the curse meet the only One who held them perfectly. There is another faithful man, in a garden, who said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38), and meant it. Who had a word that burned and a cup he begged to pass. Jesus did not edit his agony either. "Let this cup pass from me", and then, "nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will." (26:39) He went all the way down into the curse, became a curse for us, cried out forsaken, so that no believer in the dark would ever be alone in it. Jeremiah's confession is a shadow of Gethsemane. Paul could write the resolution Jeremiah could not yet see: "afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; struck down, but not destroyed." (2 Corinthians 4:8-9) Struck down. He grants it. But not destroyed. The fire that burned in Jeremiah's bones was God refusing to let him go even while it cost him everything.

Faithfulness wounded him and held him.

## The Yoke and the False Prophets
*The comforting lie, and the man it kills*

**Text:** Jeremiah 27:1-15; 28:1-17 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 6:14 · Ezekiel 13:10 · 2 Timothy 4:3-4 · Galatians 1:8-9

God tells Jeremiah to make a yoke, the heavy wooden bar laid across the neck of an ox, and to wear it through the streets of Jerusalem. It is a sermon you can see. The message is the most unwelcome one a free nation could hear: bend your neck to Babylon.

**The yoke as discipline**
The word is plain and it is offensive. "Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and live." (Jeremiah 27:12) Submission to the empire that is coming is not surrender to be resisted, it is God's own discipline to be accepted. "I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar… any nation or kingdom that will not serve him… I will punish that nation with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence." (27:6-8) The conquest is not Babylon's triumph over God. It is God's instrument. And so the obedient response is the humiliating one: wear the yoke, serve, live. There is mercy in the yoke. It is the path to survival. But it costs everything a proud people built their identity on, independence, the temple, the throne, the story that they could not fall.

**The comfortable lie**
Into that hard word steps a prophet with a better one. Hananiah, and notice he speaks in the name of the LORD, with full conviction, in the temple, before the priests. "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon. Within two years I will bring back to this place all the vessels…" (28:2-3) And to make the sermon visible, he takes the wooden yoke off Jeremiah's neck and breaks it. (28:10) Peace in two years. Restoration is near. The crisis is overblown. It is everything the people want to hear, and it is a lie.

This is the oldest sin of false prophecy, and Jeremiah had already named its mechanism: "they have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace." (Jeremiah 6:14) Ezekiel saw the same builders slapping whitewash on a wall about to fall (Ezekiel 13:10). The false prophet is not usually a cynic. Hananiah may have believed himself. That is what makes it deadly. The comforting message is so much more attractive than the true one that it does not need to be sincere to spread, it only needs to be pleasant. And the lie is not neutral. It is rebellion against God dressed as good news, because it tells a doomed people to keep doing the thing that is killing them.

Watch Jeremiah's first response to Hananiah, because it is not what you expect from a prophet under attack. "Amen. May the LORD do so." (Jeremiah 28:6) He says he wishes it were true. He would love nothing more than for the yoke to be broken and the vessels returned. There is no relish in Jeremiah's hard message, no appetite for being the bearer of doom. He wants the comfortable word to be the right one. But then he names the test that separates the true prophet from the pleasant one: "the prophet who prophesies peace, when the word of that prophet comes to pass, then it will be known that the LORD has truly sent the prophet." (28:9) Time tells. The pleasant prophecy is cheap to make and expensive to verify, and Hananiah will not survive the verification.

**The lie kills its prophet**
Jeremiah's answer is quiet and terrible. God sends him back: you have broken a wooden yoke, "but you have made in their place bars of iron." (28:13) The lie did not lighten the burden. It made it heavier, because false comfort that delays the necessary submission turns a survivable discipline into an iron one. And then the verdict on Hananiah himself: "this year you shall die, because you have uttered rebellion against the LORD." (28:16) "In that same year, in the seventh month, the prophet Hananiah died." (28:17) Within the year. The man who promised two years of peace did not live out one. The comforting lie killed its own prophet.

And I have to ask the uncomfortable question of myself before I ask it of anyone in a pulpit. Whose preaching do we reward? Paul saw exactly where this goes: "the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions." (2 Timothy 4:3-4) We do not accumulate Jeremiahs. We accumulate Hananiahs. We pay them, we promote them, we fill the rooms where someone tells us the yoke is breaking, the crisis is fake, the cost can be avoided, two more years and everything restored. And we starve the man wearing the yoke in the street. The danger in the church is rarely the obvious heretic. It is the popular prophet of cheap peace, and the appetite in us that keeps him employed.

There is one Prophet whose comfort was true precisely because he did not lighten the yoke, he took it. Jesus said, "Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me… and you will find rest for your souls." (Matthew 11:29) Not the broken yoke of false peace. A real yoke, the cross, that he wore first and wears with us. He did not say peace, peace where there was none. He went to the place of no peace and made peace by his blood. And he warned us, plainly, that the truest word would be the least popular one, that the prophets the world honors are not the ones the world should trust. "Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets." Hananiah was spoken well of. He filled the temple with applause and the people with relief, and he did not live out the year. Real comfort always passes through the truth. The kind that goes around it is the kind that dies within the year.

The comforting lie kills its prophet.

## Seek the Welfare of the City
*The harder obedience of staying when you wanted out*

**Text:** Jeremiah 29:1-14 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 27:9-10 · Daniel 6:1-3 · 1 Peter 2:11-12 · Matthew 5:44

Jeremiah writes a letter from Jerusalem to the people already dragged off to Babylon. They are sitting in the city of their conquerors, certain of one thing: this is temporary, God will bring us home soon. And God's letter takes that hope away, not to crush them, but to give them a harder and truer one.

**The command to stay**
The exiles wanted a word about leaving. God gives them a word about living. "Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters… multiply there, and do not decrease." (Jeremiah 29:5-6) Every verb assumes a future right where they did not want one. Build, that is permanence. Plant a garden, that is years before the fruit comes. Marry, have children, grow, that is generations. God is telling a homesick people to stop treating Babylon as a waiting room and start treating it as a place to live. He is taking away the lie they were clinging to, the same lie the false prophets were selling: "do not listen to your prophets… who say to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon.' For it is a lie that they are prophesying to you." (27:9-10) The quick return was the comfortable falsehood. The slow life was the obedience.

**Seek the welfare of the place that hurt you**
Then the command that should stop us cold. "Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare." (29:7) Read that again and feel the offense in it. Seek the welfare, the shalom, the flourishing, of Babylon. Pray for the city that burned your temple and chained your children. Not tolerate it. Not endure it. Seek its good, because your good is bound up with its good now. This is not collaboration with evil. It is the refusal to let exile turn you bitter and useless. It is what Daniel did in the same empire, serving the very kings who conquered him so well that "he was distinguished above all" (Daniel 6:3), without ever bending his knee to their gods. You can seek a city's welfare and refuse its idols. Both at once.

And it is exactly the posture the New Testament hands the church, which is itself an exile people. "Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that… they may see your good deeds and glorify God." (1 Peter 2:12) Sojourners and exiles, Peter calls us, seeking the welfare of a city that is not our home. It is Jesus' command stripped to the bone: "Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you." (Matthew 5:44) Pray for the city that took you. That is not a metaphor in Jeremiah. It is the literal instruction to the literal captives.

There is a sharp warning folded inside the command, too. God tells them not to listen to the prophets among them who promise a quick return, "for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you in my name." (Jeremiah 29:9) The lie was not that God would never restore them. The lie was the timeline, soon, easy, painless. False hope and true hope can sound almost identical; they differ on the cost and the wait. The prophets of the quick return were not denying God's faithfulness. They were denying that faithfulness would take seventy years to arrive, and that denial is what made them liars.

**The hope that costs seventy years**
And only after the hard command does the famous comfort come, and it lands completely differently once you see what it cost to get there. "I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope." (29:11) We put that verse on graduation cards. We rip it out of a letter to prisoners of war and use it to promise people their preferred outcome. But look at the timeline God attaches to it one verse earlier: "When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you and fulfill to you my promise." (29:10) Seventy years. Not seventy days. Most of the people reading the letter would die in Babylon. The future and the hope were real, and they were generations away. The good plan ran straight through a lifetime of exile. God's promise is not a shortcut around the hard place. It is faithfulness on the far side of it.

I have to confess how badly I want the other version. I want the God who gets me out, not the God who tells me to build a house in the middle of the thing I was begging to escape. I have prayed for rescue when God was calling me to plant a garden. We treat every hard season as a waiting room, refusing to invest, refusing to love the people God put us among, holding our breath for the return, and we miss the whole life God was giving us right there. The exile was not a delay before the real life. It was where the real life was supposed to be lived.

This is the God who would one day do the hardest staying of all. He did not rescue us from a distance. He came into the occupied city, into the exile of flesh and death, and sought our welfare at the cost of his own, praying for the very people driving the nails. The promise of a future and a hope was finally kept not by a quick return but by a cross and an empty tomb seventy generations in the making. Build your house. Plant your garden. Pray for the city. The God who keeps his word across seventy years is keeping it still.

Pray for the city that took you.

## A Covenant on the Heart
*The promise to write the law where the breaking happens*

**Text:** Jeremiah 31:31-34 · **Supporting:** Exodus 24:7-8 · Ezekiel 36:26-27 · Luke 22:20 · Hebrews 8:8-12

In a book full of collapse, ruin, and judgment that came true, four verses sit like a door cut into a wall of grief. After thirty chapters of betrayal and consequence, God promises something he has never promised before, a covenant unlike the one his people kept breaking.

**A new covenant, not the old one**
God names the failure directly. "Behold, the days are coming… when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel… not like the covenant that I made with their fathers… my covenant that they broke, though I was their husband." (Jeremiah 31:31-32) He is pointing back to Sinai, to the day Israel stood at the mountain and said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do" (Exodus 24:7), and Moses threw the blood of the covenant on the people. They meant it. And they broke it, not because the law was bad, but because the law written on stone could command the heart without changing it. That is the diagnosis under the whole book of Jeremiah. The problem was never the commandment. The problem was the heart that received it. A perfect law handed to a stubborn heart produces only a documented failure.

**The law written where the breaking happens**
So God promises to move the location of the law. "I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts." (Jeremiah 31:33) Not on tablets they will violate, on the heart itself, the very place the violation begins. This is the only thing that could possibly work, and it is the one thing the law could never do. The law could tell you what to love. It could not make you love it. A command posted outside a person can restrain the hand and condemn the failure, but it cannot reach down and change the wanting that drives both. That is what the old covenant was, a perfect standard handed to an unchanged heart, which left the desire exactly where it found it. God now promises to stop merely commanding the heart and start rewriting it. God now promises to do the impossible thing: to change the wanting, not just the commanding. Ezekiel heard the same promise in different words: "I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes." (Ezekiel 36:26-27) Cause you to walk. The obedience itself becomes a gift, not a demand. And the result is intimacy without a middleman: "they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest." (Jeremiah 31:34) Not know about. Know.

**The foundation underneath it all**
But none of that, not the new heart, not the writing, not the knowing, is the foundation. God saves the foundation for last, and stakes everything on it. "For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more." (Jeremiah 31:34) That little word for carries the whole weight. Why will the law finally take in a heart it never took before? Because the sin underneath has been dealt with first. The covenant does not begin with a demand for performance. It begins with the removal of the debt. I will remember their sin no more, said by the one God who forgets nothing, who knew Jeremiah in the womb, who counts the dead in chapter 52 with exact precision. This God chooses, by sovereign will, to hold the record of your sin no longer. Not overlooked. Not minimized. Remembered no more.

And I have to be honest that this is the promise I most struggle to believe, because I keep trying to be saved by the old covenant. I keep trying to do all that the LORD has spoken, and I keep documenting my own failure, and then I treat my failure as the reason God must still be holding the file. We are stone-tablet people by instinct. We think the change has to come from us white-knuckling the law into our behavior. Jeremiah says no. The change comes from God writing it on the inside, and the writing rests on a forgiveness that came first. You cannot earn your way into the new covenant. You can only receive it.

And notice the order, because we get it backwards constantly. We assume forgiveness is the reward at the end of a changed life, clean yourself up, and then God will forget your sin. The covenant runs the other direction. The forgiveness comes first, as the foundation, and the changed life grows up out of it. "For I will forgive" is the ground, not the goal. We spend our days trying to produce the heart of flesh so that God will pardon us, when God says he pardons us so that the heart of flesh can grow. The sequence is the whole gospel. Mercy first. Transformation second. Never the reverse.

And we know exactly when and how it was inaugurated, because the One who fulfills it told us at a table. He took the cup and said, "This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood." (Luke 22:20) The new covenant Jeremiah saw from six centuries away, sins remembered no more, the law on the heart, Jesus opened in his own blood. The writer of Hebrews quotes this exact passage in full and says of it: "In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete." (Hebrews 8:13) What Israel could not keep, Christ keeps, for them and in them. The blood Moses threw on the people only marked them. The blood of Christ changes them. He carried the sin God promised to remember no more, all the way into the grave, and left it there.

He will remember sin no more.

## Buying the Field
*Money spent on a future no one could see*

**Text:** Jeremiah 32:1-15 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 32:24-25 · Hebrews 11:1 · Romans 4:18-21 · 2 Corinthians 4:18

The setting is the worst possible moment for a real-estate purchase. Babylon's army surrounds Jerusalem. The fall is months away and inevitable. Jeremiah himself is locked in the court of the guard for preaching that the city is finished. And in that moment God tells him to buy a field.

**The command that made no sense**
The instruction comes wrapped in absurdity. Jeremiah's cousin Hanamel comes to the prison and offers him a field in Anathoth, land in territory the Babylonians already control or soon will, land no sane person would buy. And God tells him to do it. "Buy my field that is at Anathoth… for the right of possession and redemption is yours; buy it for yourself." (Jeremiah 32:7-8) So Jeremiah does it by the book. He weighs out the silver, seventeen shekels (32:9). He signs the deed, seals it, has it witnessed, and, this is the detail that matters, he has the deeds placed in an earthenware jar "that they may last for a long time." (32:14) Every step is deliberate. He is not buying a field he expects to use next week. He is spending real money to create a document meant to survive a national catastrophe, so that it can be honored on the far side of a destruction he himself has been promising. This is not denial. Jeremiah of all people knows the city is going to burn. He buys the field anyway.

**The reason: a word about the future**
And he says so to God, plainly. He prays back the very thing that makes the purchase look insane: "Behold, the siege mounds have come up to the city to take it… what you spoke has come to pass, and behold, you see it. Yet you, O Lord GOD, have said to me, 'Buy the field for money and get witnesses', though the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans." (32:24-25) He names the contradiction out loud. The city is falling, and you told me to buy land in it. And God answers with the only thing that could make the purchase rational, a promise about a future no one can see. "Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land." (32:15) The field is not an investment in current conditions. It is a wager on a word. The deed in the jar is a piece of paper that only makes sense if God is telling the truth about a restoration that, right now, every visible fact denies.

This is the very definition of faith, not optimism, not denial, but action staked on the word of God against the evidence of the eyes. "Faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen." (Hebrews 11:1) It is Abraham's posture exactly: "in hope he believed against hope… he did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead." (Romans 4:18-19) Abraham believed in a son against a dead womb. Jeremiah believed in a harvest against a burning field. Both put their money where the promise was, not where the circumstances were. "We look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen." (2 Corinthians 4:18)

And do not miss what God allows Jeremiah to feel along the way. After he buys the field, before he gets the explanation, Jeremiah prays one of the great prayers of Scripture, and it ends in honest bewilderment, he is not pretending the purchase makes sense to him. He obeyed first and questioned after. That is the actual texture of faith, and it is worth seeing clearly, because we imagine faith means the action feels obvious. It rarely does. Jeremiah signed the deed without understanding it and then took his confusion to God. The obedience did not wait for the clarity. The clarity came, when it came, on the far side of the obedience.

**The faith that costs money**
Now I have to let this land on me, because I admire this kind of faith in the abstract and almost never practice it. The thing about Jeremiah's faith is that it cost him seventeen shekels. It was not a feeling. It was a transaction. We are good at hopeful sentiments and bad at hopeful spending, bad at making decisions, with our money and our years and our actual lives, that only make sense if God's promises are true. We hedge. We keep our resources liquid in case God does not come through. We say we believe in the future God promised, and then we invest entirely in the world we can see. Jeremiah signed the deed in the dark. Faith that costs nothing is not the faith of Jeremiah 32.

And here is the test for us, the one I keep failing. We will say we trust God's promises, and then arrange our entire lives so that we never have to. We keep an exit. We hedge the bet. We refuse the kind of decision that would leave us exposed and foolish if the promise turned out to be false. Jeremiah's deed in the jar was a decision he could not undo, made public, sealed, witnessed, a bet he could not quietly walk back if the harvest never came. That is what belief looks like when it stops being a sentiment and becomes a transaction.

And there is a deeper field being bought here. Because what does it look like for God himself to spend a price on a future no eye could see? It looks like a cross. God paid, not seventeen shekels but his own Son, to purchase a people and a new creation when every visible fact said the field was lost, when the body was in the tomb and the disciples had scattered and the promise looked dead. "You were bought with a price." Christ paid for a restoration the world could not see, and sealed the deed in his blood, and put it where it would last. Jeremiah's jar in the ground is a shadow of an empty tomb. The God who told a prisoner to buy a field in a doomed city is the God who buys back a doomed people for a future they cannot yet see.

He paid for a promised future.

## The City Falls
*The long-warned word, finally and terribly true*

**Text:** Jeremiah 39:1-10 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 7:4 · Jeremiah 38:17-18 · Lamentations 1:1 · Galatians 6:7

For forty years Jeremiah said it was coming, and for forty years they called him a traitor, a liar, a doom-monger. Jeremiah 39 is the chapter where the talking stops. The wall breaks.

**The siege ends**
The account is spare and merciless, almost like a military log, and the bareness is the point. "In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah… Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem and besieged it. In the eleventh year… on the ninth day of the month, a breach was made in the city." (Jeremiah 39:1-2) Eighteen months of siege, eighteen months of starvation behind those walls the people thought God would never let fall, and then the wall is breached and the Babylonian officials come in and sit in the middle gate. The unthinkable has happened. The temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the charm they chanted in chapter 7, did not hold. "Do not trust in these deceptive words," Jeremiah had warned them at that very gate (7:4), and now the deceptive words are exposed by the rubble. Every illusion that ritual or politics could hold back the consequence of covenant betrayal dies in a single sentence: a breach was made in the city.

**Zedekiah's eyes**
And then the camera narrows to one man, and the horror becomes personal. King Zedekiah tries to flee by night and is overtaken in the plains of Jericho. He is brought before Nebuchadnezzar, and the sentence is carried out with deliberate cruelty. "The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes… Then he put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains." (39:6-7) Read the sequence God allowed. The last thing Zedekiah ever saw was the death of his sons. They made certain of it, killed the boys in front of him, and then blinded him, so that the final image burned into his darkness forever would be that one. And this was avoidable. Jeremiah had gone to this king and given him God's plain offer: "If you will surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then your life shall be spared… But if you do not surrender… this city shall be given into the hand of the Chaldeans." (38:17-18) Zedekiah was afraid of what people would think. He chose his reputation over the warning. And he watched his sons die for it.

The temple was burned, the houses leveled, the city walls broken down, and the people carried away, "all the rest of the people who were left in the city" (39:9), the poorest left behind to tend the vines. The book of Lamentations is the funeral that follows: "How lonely sits the city that was full of people. How like a widow has she become." (Lamentations 1:1) The prophet was vindicated, and there is no triumph in it. Being right about a catastrophe is its own kind of grief.

And notice the chapter cannot end on the ruin alone, because even here God keeps a promise to one man. In the middle of the wreckage, the word comes to spare Ebed-melech, the foreigner who had pulled Jeremiah out of the cistern: "I will surely save you… because you have put your trust in me, declares the LORD." (39:18) The city that trusted the temple as a charm falls. The Cushite official who actually trusted God is delivered. The contrast is deliberate and it is the whole point of the book in miniature, the difference between trusting the sacred thing and trusting the holy God. The walls came down on the first. Mercy came down on the second.

**The line we do not want to read**
And here is the verse the whole Bible refuses to let us delete, the one we squirm under: "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that he will also reap." (Galatians 6:7) That is the law under Jeremiah 39. Judah sowed injustice and idolatry and the casual assumption that God's patience meant God's approval, and the harvest came. Not because God is cruel, but because consequence is real and a holy God will not pretend otherwise forever. We do not like this chapter because it tells us the warnings were not bluffs. The grace of God is enormous and the patience of God is long, and neither of them is the same as the absence of consequence. We have built a sentimental faith that treats every warning as negotiable and every delay as a cancellation. Judah believed that too. The wall still broke.

I cannot preach this chapter from a safe distance, because I know the Zedekiah in me, the part that hears the truth, agrees the truth is true, and still chooses the reputation, the comfort, the fear of what people will say, over the costly obedience the truth requires. He did not disbelieve Jeremiah. He was afraid. And the fear cost him his sons and his sight. The most dangerous unbelief is not denial. It is the agreement that never surrenders.

And yet, even here, the gospel is not absent, it is hidden. Because there is another King who was bound, and led out, and made to watch the consequence of sin land in full. The difference is that Jesus suffered the harvest he did not sow. Zedekiah reaped his own field. Christ reaped ours, went under the breached wall of God's judgment, took the eyes-put-out darkness of forsakenness, "became sin who knew no sin," so that the consequence we had coming would fall on him. The ruin of Jerusalem shows us what our sin actually earns. The cross shows us where it actually went, for everyone who will surrender instead of fleeing in the dark.

The word warned came finally true.

## The Ruin and the Lifted Head
*The honest record of the cost, and a small light kept burning in the dark*

**Text:** Jeremiah 52:1-34 · **Supporting:** Lamentations 3:21-23 · 2 Samuel 7:16 · Genesis 50:20 · Matthew 1:11-12

The book of Jeremiah ends not with a sermon but with an inventory. Chapter 52 is a ledger, it counts the dead, the burned, the carried-away, and it refuses to round the numbers down. And then, in its very last verses, it does something almost no one expects. It lifts a head.

**The honest accounting of ruin**
The chapter will not let us look away from the cost. It records the breach of the wall, the burning of the temple, the king's sons slaughtered and his eyes put out, and then it does the bookkeeping. The bronze pillars of the temple broken up and carried to Babylon. The pots, the shovels, the basins, the smallest implements of worship inventoried and hauled off (Jeremiah 52:17-23). The exact count of the exiles in three deportations: "all the persons were 4,600." (52:30) And the named men of Judah executed at Riblah, the chief priest, the second priest, the officers, the scribe (52:24-27). Names. Numbers. Sober, deliberate precision. The Bible could have softened this. It does not. It writes down the cost of Judah's sin to the last basin and the last body, because grief that gets rounded off is grief denied, and God will not let his people pretend the wages of their betrayal were small. This is the same honesty that produced Lamentations sitting right beside it, the refusal to rush past the ruin to the comfort.

**The lifted head**
And then, after fifty-two chapters of weeping and warning and rubble, the final paragraph turns. "In the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah… Evil-merodach king of Babylon… graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison. And he spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat above the seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon." (Jeremiah 52:31-32) The imprisoned king of David's line is brought up out of the dungeon, given clothes, given a seat at the table, given honor above the other captive kings, "and for his allowance, a regular allowance was given him by the king… every day a portion until the day of his death." (52:34) It is small. It is not a return, not a restoration, not a throne in Jerusalem. It is one freed prisoner and a daily meal. But in the dark of the exile it is everything, because it means the line of David is not extinguished. The lamp is low, but the lamp is lit. God had sworn to David, "your throne shall be established forever" (2 Samuel 7:16), and at the end of the bleakest book in the prophets, that promise is hanging by a single freed king and a portion of bread, and hanging there, it holds.

This is the God Lamentations confessed from the floor of the same ruin: "But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: the steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning." (Lamentations 3:21-23) Even in the inventory of disaster, mercy keeps a head lifted.

And the placement of this ending is no accident. The story of Jehoiachin's release in chapter 52 is repeated almost word for word at the very end of 2 Kings, the editors of the Old Testament chose to close the entire history of the monarchy not on the burning of the temple but on a freed king and a daily ration of bread. They could have ended on the ash. They ended on the allowance. That is a theological decision made in the dark, by people who had lost everything, who refused to let the final word be ruin. They had read the covenant promise to David and they bet the last sentence of their history on it: the throne would not stay empty forever, because God had sworn it would not.

**What the ending teaches us**
I need this ending, because I am tempted toward two lies and the chapter kills them both. The first lie is denial, the instinct to soften the cost of sin, to skip the ledger, to pretend the ruin was not that bad. Chapter 52 will not let me. It makes me read the count. The second lie is despair, the instinct, once I have seen the full cost, to conclude that it is over, that the failure was final, that God is done. The last paragraph will not let me do that either. It lifts a head in the dark precisely so I cannot. We tend to think honesty about ruin and hope for restoration are opposites. Jeremiah 52 holds them together: full accounting of the cost, and a small light kept burning. That is not contradiction. That is faith with its eyes open.

And the lifted head goes somewhere. Open the New Testament to its first page and the genealogy of Jesus runs straight through this exact moment: "and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. And after the deportation to Babylon, Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel." (Matthew 1:11-12) Jechoniah is Jehoiachin, the freed prisoner of Jeremiah 52. The genealogy of Christ runs through the dungeon. The small lifted head at the end of the weeping prophet's book is a link in the chain that ends at Bethlehem, and at a cross, and at an empty tomb. What men meant for ruin, God meant for the saving of many (Genesis 50:20). The Son of David who finally takes the throne forever comes down precisely this line, through the deportation, through the prison, through the daily portion of bread. God kept the lamp lit through the darkest book in Scripture, because the true King was coming, and nothing in Babylon could put out that light.

Ruin recorded, yet a head lifted.
